title: Explain the Circuit Breaker pattern states (Closed/Open/Half-Open), how you tune thresholds/timeouts/reset-time, whether the breaker can be a single point of failure, how to prevent cascading failures across chained breakers, pitfalls in async/Kafka systems, the fallback-depends-on-failing-service trap, adaptive breakers, and when a breaker is harmful.
shortTitle: Circuit Breaker pattern — Closed, Open, Half-Open states, tuning, pitfalls, and when it is harmful
topicTitle: Behavioral — Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template

s1_definition.profdef: The Circuit Breaker pattern is a stability pattern that wraps a call to a remote or fragile dependency and monitors it for failures. When failures exceed a configured threshold, the breaker trips to an Open state and short-circuits further calls, failing fast instead of waiting for timeouts. After a reset timeout it moves to Half-Open, where it allows a few trial calls through. If those succeed, it closes and resumes normal traffic; if they fail, it reopens. This protects both the caller and the struggling dependency from cascading failure.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the electrical circuit breaker in Rajesh's house. Normally electricity flows freely — that is Closed. But if there is a dangerous surge, the breaker trips and cuts the power so the house does not burn down — that is Open. After some time Rajesh flips it back carefully to test if things are safe — that is Half-Open. If the lights work fine, he leaves it on (back to Closed); if sparks fly again, it trips immediately. In banking, the "electricity" is a call to the CIBIL credit-score service. If CIBIL is down and every loan request keeps waiting thirty seconds and then failing, our whole loan service grinds to a halt. The circuit breaker trips, so loan requests fail fast with a fallback instead of dragging everything down.
s1_definition.oneliner: Closed means try normally, Open means fail fast and do not call, Half-Open means cautiously test if the dependency has recovered.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Circuit Breaker pattern is a stability pattern that wraps a call to a remote or fragile dependency and monitors it for failures. When failures exceed a configured threshold, the breaker trips to an Open state and short-circuits further calls, failing fast instead of waiting for timeouts. After a reset timeout it moves to Half-Open, where it allows a few trial calls through. If those succeed, it closes and resumes normal traffic; if they fail, it reopens. This protects both the caller and the struggling dependency from cascading failure.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the electrical circuit breaker in Rajesh's house. Normally electricity flows freely — that is Closed. But if there is a dangerous surge, the breaker trips and cuts the power so the house does not burn down — that is Open. After some time Rajesh flips it back carefully to test if things are safe — that is Half-Open. If the lights work fine, he leaves it on (back to Closed); if sparks fly again, it trips immediately. In banking, the "electricity" is a call to the CIBIL credit-score service. If CIBIL is down and every loan request keeps waiting thirty seconds and then failing, our whole loan service grinds to a halt. The circuit breaker trips, so loan requests fail fast with a fallback instead of dragging everything down.

**One line to remember:** Closed means try normally, Open means fail fast and do not call, Half-Open means cautiously test if the dependency has recovered.

sections.s2_technical:
The breaker has three states. In **Closed** state, calls flow through normally and the breaker counts failures. It typically uses either a count-based window (last N calls) or a time-based window (calls in the last T seconds). When the failure rate crosses a threshold — say fifty percent of the last twenty calls failed — the breaker transitions to **Open**. In Open state, every call is immediately rejected with an exception like `CallNotPermittedException` or routed to a fallback, without touching the real dependency. After a configured wait duration, the breaker moves to **Half-Open**, where it permits a limited number of trial calls. If those trial calls succeed above a success threshold, it transitions back to Closed; otherwise it returns to Open.

Tuning matters a lot. The **failure threshold** should reflect how fragile the dependency is — a fifty percent failure rate over a sliding window of twenty calls is a common starting point. The **call timeout** must be shorter than the client's patience; a slow call that eventually succeeds is often worse than a fast failure, so slow calls above a duration are counted as failures. The **reset/wait duration in open state** controls how long you stop hammering a sick service — too short and you re-trip constantly, too long and you stay down after the dependency recovers. In Resilience4j you configure this with something like `CircuitBreakerConfig.custom().failureRateThreshold(50).slidingWindowSize(20).waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3).build()`.

Can the breaker itself be a single point of failure? If you implement one shared breaker instance guarding a resource for the whole fleet and that logic has a bug or a shared mutable counter under contention, yes, it can become a bottleneck or a point of failure. The mitigation is to keep breaker state per-instance (each service node has its own in-memory breaker) or use a well-tested library like Resilience4j rather than hand-rolling. The breaker should be lightweight and not depend on an external system to decide its own state.

To prevent cascading failures across chained breakers, you combine the breaker with timeouts, bulkheads (isolating thread pools so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads), and sensible fallbacks. If service A calls B calls C, and C is down, C's breaker trips and returns a fast fallback, which lets B's breaker stay healthy, which keeps A responsive. Without breakers, C's slowness would pile up threads in B, then in A, and the whole chain would collapse.

There are real pitfalls. In **async / Kafka** systems, the breaker concept is subtler because there is no synchronous caller waiting for a response. Tripping a breaker on a Kafka consumer usually means pausing consumption or sending messages to a retry topic or dead letter queue rather than throwing an exception to a caller. A common mistake is wrapping the producer send in a breaker but forgetting that messages still accumulate in the topic, so when the breaker closes you get a thundering herd. The **fallback-depends-on-the-failing-service trap** is another classic: your fallback for a failed balance lookup reads from a cache that is populated by the same failing service, so the fallback is also stale or empty. The fallback must be genuinely independent — a last-known-good value, a default, a queued retry, or a graceful degraded response.

An **adaptive breaker** goes further by adjusting its thresholds dynamically based on observed latency and error patterns, rather than fixed numbers. This is useful when traffic varies wildly, but it adds complexity and can behave unpredictably, so most teams start with static thresholds and only move to adaptive when they have strong monitoring.

A breaker is **harmful** when it guards a call that is actually cheap, local, and reliable — you add latency and complexity for no benefit. It is also harmful when the fallback is worse than a brief delay, when the threshold is so sensitive that it trips on normal transient blips, or when it hides a real bug that you should fix rather than route around. In short, a breaker protects against a flaky external dependency; it is not a substitute for correctness.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's loan approval service calls an external CIBIL credit-score API for every loan application. When CIBIL has an outage, each call hangs for thirty seconds before timing out. Because loan requests come in continuously, threads pile up waiting on CIBIL, and soon the entire loan service stops responding — even requests that do not need CIBIL. One sick dependency is taking down a healthy service. This is the cascading failure that a circuit breaker prevents. When CIBIL starts failing, the breaker trips and loan requests fail fast with a sensible fallback instead of hanging.

Problem 2 — Simply failing is not acceptable in banking; we still need to make a decision. So when the breaker is Open, we fall back to a conservative rule: approve only small loans up to a safe limit using the customer's internal account history, and mark larger ones for manual review. Crucially, this fallback must not itself call CIBIL — otherwise we fall into the fallback-depends-on-the-failing-service trap. Our fallback uses only our own database.

In the mini-project we will build a small circuit breaker from scratch (so the mechanics are visible) that wraps calls to a `CibilClient`. The breaker tracks failures, trips to Open after a threshold, waits, then tries Half-Open. We will simulate CIBIL being down for several calls, watch the breaker trip, see fast-fail fallbacks, then simulate CIBIL recovering and watch the breaker close again. Rajesh applies for a loan while CIBIL is healthy, then CIBIL goes down and Priya's request hits the fallback.

The code contains: a `CibilClient` that can be toggled healthy or down; a `CircuitBreaker` class with the three states; a `LoanService` that calls through the breaker and provides a fallback; and a `main` that drives the scenarios.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one healthy loan request for Rajesh, then CIBIL goes down for several requests, then CIBIL recovers.

Step 1: Rajesh applies for a three lakh loan while CIBIL is healthy. The breaker is Closed, so `allowRequest` returns true. `cibil.fetchScore` returns 780, `recordSuccess` resets the failure count, and the loan is approved normally.

Step 2: CIBIL is switched to down. The first request calls `fetchScore`, which throws. The catch block calls `recordFailure`, incrementing the failure count to one, and the fallback approves the small loan using internal history. The breaker is still Closed.

Step 3: Two more requests fail the same way, pushing the failure count to three, which equals the threshold. On that third failure, the breaker transitions to Open and records the time. From now on calls are short-circuited.

Step 4: The next request finds the breaker Open. `allowRequest` returns false immediately — no call to CIBIL at all — and the fallback runs instantly. This is the fast-fail behaviour that protects the service.

Step 5: After the reset period of just over two seconds, CIBIL is switched back to healthy and a new request arrives. `allowRequest` sees the reset time has passed, moves to Half-Open, and permits one trial call. `fetchScore` now succeeds, `recordSuccess` runs, and the breaker closes. Normal service is restored.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Circuit Breaker pattern is a stability pattern that wraps a call to a fragile dependency and watches it for failures. It has three states. In Closed state, calls flow normally and the breaker counts failures. When failures cross a threshold, it trips to Open, where it fails fast and does not call the dependency at all. After a reset timeout it moves to Half-Open, where it lets a few trial calls through — if they succeed it closes again, and if they fail it reopens.

In my banking project the loan approval service depended on the external CIBIL credit-score API. During a CIBIL outage every call hung for thirty seconds and threads piled up, which threatened to take down the whole loan service. I put a circuit breaker around that call so that once CIBIL started failing consistently, the breaker tripped and loan requests failed fast and fell back to a conservative internal rule instead of hanging. That single change stopped one sick dependency from cascading into a full outage.

On tuning, I set the failure rate threshold around fifty percent over a sliding window, kept the per-call timeout short because a slow call is often worse than a fast failure, and chose a wait duration in the open state that was long enough to give CIBIL room to recover but short enough that we resumed quickly. I also used bulkheads to isolate the thread pool so the breaker plus bulkhead together prevented thread exhaustion.

The two traps I always call out are the fallback-depends-on-the-failing-service trap and async systems. My fallback used only our own database and never called CIBIL, because a fallback that depends on the broken service is useless. And in Kafka-based flows a breaker does not throw to a caller; instead you pause consumption or route to a retry or dead letter topic, and you have to watch for a thundering herd when the breaker closes. Finally, a breaker is harmful when it guards something cheap and reliable, when the threshold is so sensitive it trips on normal blips, or when it hides a real bug that you should actually fix. I used a battle-tested library, Resilience4j, and kept breaker state per instance so the breaker itself never became a single point of failure.
